You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary at /workspace/dataset/test15_executable.
DO NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk anyway).
DO NOT use `strings`, `objdump`, `nm`, `gdb`, or any binary/symbol inspection. Behavioral probing via command-line arguments ONLY.

The binary's driver program is exactly this:

  inflection::Inflector::initialize();
  std::vector<std::string> results;
  for (int i = 1; i < argc && i <= 5; i++) {
      std::string word = argv[i];
      results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::pluralize(word));
      results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::camelize(word));
      if (i % 2 == 0) results.push_back(inflection::Inflector::underscore(word));
  }
  for (const auto& r : results) std::cout << r << std::endl;
  if (argc > 1) {
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::isPlural(argv[1]) << std::endl;
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::isSingular(argv[1]) << std::endl;
      std::cout << inflection::Inflector::demodulize("Module::" + std::string(argv[1])) << std::endl;
  }

So to observe a function on an arbitrary word W:
  - pluralize(W)  -> line 1 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - camelize(W)   -> line 2 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - underscore(W) -> `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable dummy "W"` prints: pluralize(dummy), camelize(dummy), pluralize(W), camelize(W), underscore(W), then isPlural/isSingular/demodulize of "dummy". So underscore(W) is line 5.
  - isPlural(W)   -> line 3 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"` (prints as 0/1 since it's a bool via operator<<)
  - isSingular(W) -> line 4 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`
  - demodulize("Module::" + W) -> line 5 of `/workspace/dataset/test15_executable "W"`

Run MANY probes (hundreds). Use bash loops. Quote arguments properly. Capture stderr too (2>&1 separately from stdout when it matters) and capture exit codes.
Be systematic: form a hypothesis, then design inputs that DISCRIMINATE between competing hypotheses, then confirm.
Report the exact rule as precise pseudocode operating on BYTES (the C++ code uses std::string = bytes; the "C" locale means std::toupper/tolower only affect ASCII a-z/A-Z). Explicitly test non-ASCII UTF-8 input to confirm byte-level behavior.


=== ADVERSARIAL CROSS-CHECK: driver_and_argv ===

Another engineer probed the `driver_and_argv` behavior of /workspace/dataset/test15_executable and produced this spec. Your job is to FALSIFY it. Assume it is subtly wrong. Design and run inputs specifically engineered to break it, then report every discrepancy between the spec's prediction and the binary's actual output.

SPEC PSEUDOCODE:
// Driver / CLI behavior of /workspace/dataset/test15_executable
// All output on STDOUT (fd 1). Nothing is ever written to stderr except the
// uncaught-exception abort message described below. argv[0] is never used.
// stdin is never read. No flag/option parsing whatsoever: "-h", "--help",
// "--", "-" are treated as ordinary words.

main(argc, argv):
    Inflector::initialize()          // produces NO output
    results = []                     // std::vector<std::string>, buffered

    // NOTE: loop guard is `i < argc && i <= 5`, so at most args 1..5 are used.
    N = min(argc - 1, 5)             // number of processed args
    for i in 1 .. N:                 // 1-based index into argv
        word = argv[i]               // raw bytes, no copy/trim/decoding
        results.push_back(pluralize(word))
        results.push_back(camelize(word))
        if i % 2 == 0:               // i.e. only i == 2 and i == 4
            results.push_back(underscore(word))

    for r in results:                // ALL buffered results printed FIRST
        write(stdout, r); write(stdout, "
")   // std::endl => '
' + flush

    if argc > 1:                     // trailing 3 lines, only if >=1 arg given
        write(stdout, isPlural(argv[1])   ? "1" : "0"); write "
"
        write(stdout, isSingular(argv[1]) ? "1" : "0"); write "
"
        // no std::boolalpha => bools print as the bytes '0' / '1'
        write(stdout, demodulize("Module::" + argv[1])); write "
"
    return 0

// ---------------- LINE LAYOUT ----------------
// Let N = min(argc-1, 5).
// TOTAL_LINES = 0                                      if N == 0
//             = 2*N + floor(N/2) + 3                   if N >= 1
//   N: 0 1 2 3  4  5 (and 5 for every argc-1 >= 5)
//   L: 0 5 8 10 13 15
//
// Line order (1-based), for N >= 1:
//   block(i) for i = 1..N, concatenated in order:
//        pluralize(argv[i])
//        camelize(argv[i])
//        underscore(argv[i])        // present ONLY when i is even (i==2, i==4)
//   then exactly 3 trailing lines:
//        isPlural(argv[1])   as '0'/'1'
//        isSingular(argv[1]) as '0'/'1'
//        demodulize("Module::" + argv[1])
//
// Concrete absolute line indices:
//   N=1: 1 plur(a1) 2 cam(a1) | 3 isPlural 4 isSingular 5 demodulize
//   N=2: 1 plur(a1) 2 cam(a1) 3 plur(a2) 4 cam(a2) 5 und(a2) | 6,7,8
//   N=3: ... 6 plur(a3) 7 cam(a3) | 8,9,10
//   N=4: ... 8 plur(a4) 9 cam(a4) 10 und(a4) | 11,12,13
//   N=5: ... 11 plur(a5) 12 cam(a5) | 13,14,15
// Args 6, 7, 8, ... 200 are read from argv but completely ignored.

// ---------------- BYTES / NEWLINES ----------------
// Every emitted line is terminated by exactly one 0x0A. There is a trailing
// newline after the final line. With 0 args the output is 0 bytes (no newline).
// Embedded '
' / '	' / ' ' inside an argument are passed through verbatim and
// therefore split what looks like one "line" into several physical lines.

// ---------------- EXIT CODES ----------------
// exit 0 in every normal case (including 0 args, empty args in positions >= 2).
// CRASH (uncaught std::out_of_range from demodulize's substr) iff:
//        argv[1] == ""  OR  argv[1] ends with the byte ':'
//   (because s = "Module::"+argv[1]; pos = s.rfind(':'); s.substr(pos+2)
//    and pos+2 > s.size() exactly when the last ':' is the final byte)
//   -> std::terminate -> SIGABRT (signal 6), shell-observed exit status 134,
//      core dumped. All previously produced lines (the whole results vector
//      PLUS the isPlural and isSingular lines) are already flushed to stdout
//      before the abort, because std::endl flushes each line.
//   stderr on crash, byte-exact (147 bytes, two lines):
//     "terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::out_of_range'
"
//     "  what():  basic_string::substr: __pos (which is P) > this->size() (which is S)
"
//   where S = 8 + len(argv[1]) and P = S + 1.
//   (Note the two spaces after "what():" and after the colon.)

// ---------------- LOCALE ----------------
// Output is byte-identical under LC_ALL = C, POSIX, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8,
// de_DE.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8. No locale is ever imbue'd; case mapping is plain
// ASCII (Turkish 'I'/'i' behave exactly as in C). Non-ASCII UTF-8 bytes
// (>= 0x80) and invalid UTF-8 (e.g. 0xFF 0xFE) pass through untouched, so all
// string handling is byte-wise, not codepoint-wise.

CLAIMED FINDINGS:
1. 0 args (argc==1): completely empty stdout (0 bytes), empty stderr, exit 0. Inflector::initialize() prints nothing.
2. Loop guard `i < argc && i <= 5` confirmed: with 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 200 arguments the output is byte-identical to the 5-arg case; args 6+ are ignored entirely.
3. underscore() is emitted only for i==2 and i==4 (even i within 1..5). Verified: N=1 has no underscore line, N=2 has one (after arg2's camelize), N=3 still one, N=4 has two, N=5 still two.
4. Line-count formula confirmed empirically for argc-1 = 0..10: 0,5,8,10,13,15,15,15,15,15,15 == 2N+floor(N/2)+3 for N=min(argc-1,5)>=1, 0 for N=0.
5. Ordering confirmed: the whole results vector (all pluralize/camelize/underscore lines, interleaved per-argument) is printed BEFORE the three trailing lines. The trailing lines always refer to argv[1] only, never to the last arg.
6. Booleans print as the single bytes '0' and '1' (no std::boolalpha). E.g. `boxes` -> isPlural=1, isSingular=0; `people` -> 0,1.
7. Everything goes to stdout. `test15_executable cat 2>/dev/null` prints the full 5 lines; `test15_executable cat 1>/dev/null` prints nothing; `2>&1 1>/dev/null` yields 0 bytes in the success case.
8. Trailing newline: od -c shows the last byte is 
 for every non-empty output; 0-arg output is exactly 0 bytes (no lone newline).
9. Empty-string argument in position 1 CRASHES: demodulize("Module::") does substr(9) on a size-8 string -> std::out_of_range -> terminate -> SIGABRT, shell exit status 134, 'core dumped'.
10. Empty-string arguments in positions 2..5 are harmless: pluralize("")="", camelize("")="", underscore("")="" all emit empty lines, exit 0. Verified with `x ""` (8 lines, several blank) and with `"" "" ""` (crashes only because argv[1] is empty).
11. Crash is NOT limited to the empty string: any argv[1] ending in the byte ':' also crashes (":", "::", "x:", "a::", "y:") because the last ':' lands on the final index so rfind(':')+2 > size. "x::y" and "A::B::C" do not crash (they yield an empty demodulize line).
12. Buffered lines ARE flushed before the crash: `test15_executable "" a b c d e f` prints 14 lines (2 blanks for the empty arg1, blocks for a,b,c,d, then '0' and '1') and only then aborts. Same when stdout is a pipe (std::endl flushes each line).
13. Byte-exact crash stderr is 147 bytes: "terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::out_of_range'
  what():  basic_string::substr: __pos (which is 9) > this->size() (which is 8)
" for argv[1]==""; the numbers scale as size = 8+len(argv[1]), pos = size+1.
14. Exit status decomposes as 128+6 = SIGABRT; the process really is killed by signal 6, not exiting with code 134.
15. No flag parsing at all: "-h", "--help", "-", "--", "-v", "--version" are inflected like ordinary words (e.g. "--help" -> "--helps" / "--help" / demodulize "-help").
16. Args containing spaces, tabs, newlines, semicolons, and glob chars are passed through verbatim; a newline inside an arg simply produces extra physical lines.
17. Very long args work: a 100,000-byte 'a' argument yields 300,007 bytes of output (pluralize len 100001, camelize len 100000, demodulize len 99999), exit 0 — no truncation, no length limit observed.
18. argv[0] is unused: running through a symlink named /tmp/weirdname produces identical output.
19. stdin is never read: `< /dev/null` and `echo hello |` give identical output; closing stdout (`>&-`) still exits 0.
20. Locale-independent: LC_ALL in {C, POSIX, C.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8} gives byte-identical output for "I", "i", "istanbul", "ImageURL". Turkish locale does NOT produce dotted/dotless I. Plain ASCII case mapping is safe for a Rust port.
21. Byte-level (not codepoint) processing confirmed: "ÉCOLE" (c3 89 43 4f 4c 45) -> underscore = c3 89 5f 63 5f 6f 5f 6c 5f 65 ("\xc3\x89_c_o_l_e"); "café" and "日本語" pass through unchanged; invalid UTF-8 (ff fe) is passed through and gets an 's' appended by pluralize.
22. Ruled out: output interleaving per-argument with the trailing block (disproved — trailing block always last); ruled out that the trailing block uses the last argument (disproved with `boxes person ...` where line 13/14 = 1/0 matching "boxes", not "mouse"); ruled out demodulize using rfind("::")+2 (disproved by "x::y" -> "" instead of "y", so it is rfind(':')+2); ruled out any stderr usage in the success path (0 bytes captured).

CLAIMED UNCERTAINTIES:
The exact classification of the crash exit status depends on the caller: the process dies from SIGABRT (signal 6). A POSIX shell reports 134; a Rust harness using std::process would see ExitStatus::signal() == Some(6) and code() == None. A Rust port that does not throw would need an explicit choice here.
The abort message text ('terminate called after throwing an instance of ...' plus the libstdc++ substr wording, including the two spaces after 'what():') is libstdc++-specific. A Rust port cannot reproduce it verbatim unless hard-coded; only the numbers (pos = 9 + len(argv[1]), size = 8 + len(argv[1])) are derived from the input.
I did not test an argument list large enough to hit ARG_MAX, nor stdout on a full filesystem / EPIPE mid-stream (SIGPIPE behavior on a closed pipe reader was not probed).
Whether the results vector is flushed all at once vs per-line is unobservable beyond what std::endl guarantees; every line is individually flushed, which is why partial output survives the abort. I could not distinguish 'vector then loop' from 'immediate print' by output alone — only by the fact that ordering is strictly results-then-trailing-block, which both models predict.
The per-function semantics (pluralize/camelize/underscore/isPlural/isSingular/demodulize) shown in the goldens are incidental to this dimension; other dimensions own their exact rules. I only verified enough to anchor line positions (notably that demodulize == s.substr(s.rfind(':')+2) on "Module::"+argv[1], which is what causes the crash).

Also independently VERIFY a sample of these claimed goldens by actually re-running the binary:

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
